title: The brothers come for bread (Genesis 42)
hook: they bow to a man they don't recognize
carry: you don't see who it is

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharaoh's dreams: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner put in charge of Egypt's grain. Your line was store in the good years. Now the lean years arrive. Day seventy-one.

The famine spreads past Egypt, all the way to Canaan, to Jacob's tents. And Jacob hears there's grain in Egypt. He says to his sons, why are you staring at each other? Go down and buy us food, so we can live. Ten brothers go. Not Benjamin. Jacob won't let Rachel's last son out of his sight. So ten men walk into Egypt with money in their bags, and stand in line in front of the governor who sells the grain to everyone. And they bow down to him, faces to the ground. Just like the sheaves in the dream they once hated him for. Today: the man they don't recognize.
screen: `THE FAMINE REACHES CANAAN.` → `TEN BROTHERS, NOT BENJAMIN.` → `FACES TO THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: The Torah puts the whole scene in one line: "And Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew him not." How could they not know him? He was seventeen when they sold him, and now he's nearly forty. He's shaved like an Egyptian, dressed like one, speaks through an interpreter. An old explanation, passed on by Rashi, says it simply: when they sold him he had no beard, and now he had one. But there's a deeper reason. They weren't looking for him. You don't see who it is when you've decided who it can't be. And Joseph? He remembers the dreams. He speaks to them harshly. The Hebrew here is clever: he recognized them, and made himself a stranger to them, and those two verbs come from the same root. He calls them spies. They protest: we are twelve brothers, sons of one man; the youngest is with our father, and one is no more. One is no more. They're talking about him, to his face. Joseph keeps one brother, Simeon, as a hostage, and says: bring me your youngest brother. And then, thinking the governor can't understand Hebrew, the brothers say to each other: "We are verily guilty concerning our brother," we saw his distress when he pleaded with us, and we wouldn't listen. Reuben says, didn't I tell you? And Joseph, who understands every word, turns away from them and weeps. More than twenty years later, the brothers are finally talking about what they did. And the man they did it to is standing right there, listening.
screen: `JOSEPH KNEW THEM; THEY KNEW HIM NOT.` · `HE MADE HIMSELF A STRANGER.` · `ONE IS NO MORE.` · `WE ARE VERILY GUILTY.` · then, large: `HE TURNED AWAY AND WEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice someone you may have misjudged. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you've filed away. The difficult coworker. The relative you've written off. The stranger you decided about in one glance. Ask yourself what you might not be seeing. What they might be carrying, or who they might have become since. You don't have to change your mind. Just leave the door open a crack. The bell holds the time.
The brothers come for bread. Ten brothers bow to the governor of Egypt, and never see that he's the brother they sold.
screen: `THE BROTHERS COME FOR BREAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: you don't see who it is. Today, look again at one person you think you already know. Day seventy-one.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition reads this chapter as the beginning of the brothers' repair: the first time they admit aloud what they did to Joseph.

fork.setup: you're Joseph, governor of Egypt. the brothers who sold you are bowing in front of you, and they don't know who you are. what do you do?
options: tell them who you are at once.
hide who you are and test them.
have them thrown out of Egypt.
fork.reveal: he makes himself a stranger, calls them spies, keeps Simeon, and asks for Benjamin. when he hears them admit their guilt, he turns away and weeps.

original.note: Hebrew: he recognized them, and made himself a stranger. both from the root n-k-r.

trapdoor: what you thought: the brothers were fooled by a disguise.
what it means: they didn't see him because they'd decided he couldn't be there. and for the first time, they admit what they did.
what a scholar hears: 42:7 plays on n-k-r, recognize and estrange. Rashi on 42:8: he'd had no beard when sold, and now had one.

notes: 'Nearly forty': Joseph is 30 at 41:46, plus seven years of plenty and the start of famine, so about 37–38. Confirm.
Rashi on 42:8 (beard), from Yevamot 88a / Ketubot 27b. Confirm.

Reviewer edit: hook said the brothers 'laughed at' the dream; Genesis 37:8 says they hated him for it, so changed to 'hated him for'. 'Twenty years later' changed to 'more than twenty years later' (17 at the sale, about 38-39 now; Rashi counts 22 years).
